metadata.title: How to Use AI Agents in Capacitor App Development
metadata.description: Use AI agents in Capacitor app development: install Capacitor skills, connect Capgo MCP servers, and let agents add plugins, debug, build, and ship.
metadata.author: Martin Donadieu

faq.question: Which AI agents work with the Capacitor skills?
faq.answer: Any agent that supports the open skills format: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and others. Install them with bunx skills add Cap-go/capgo-skills.

faq.question: Do I still need MCP servers if I install the skills?
faq.answer: They solve different problems. Skills teach the agent how to do a task correctly. MCP servers give it live tools and data: the public Capgo MCP for docs and API discovery, and the Capgo CLI MCP for authenticated actions like uploads and builds.

faq.question: Does the agent see my signing certificates?
faq.answer: It does not need to. Capgo Build credentials are saved once with the CLI in a local credentials file and sent only for the build, then deleted after it completes. The agent triggers commands and reads logs, so keep credential files out of the repo and out of prompts.

faq.question: Do I need a Mac for the agent to build iOS apps?
faq.answer: Not with cloud builds. The agent can run a Capgo Build request from Windows or Linux, read the logs, and iterate on fixes. You still need an Apple Developer account and signing credentials.

faq.question: Can an agent ship a live update without app review?
faq.answer: It can upload a web bundle to a channel with the Capgo CLI. Live updates must stay within store rules, which allow updating web code but not changing the app's main purpose. Changes to native code still go through a store release.

blocks.text: To use AI agents in Capacitor app development, give the agent two things it lacks by default: procedural knowledge of Capacitor's native side, through installable

and a CLI it can run. With Capgo's open-source Capacitor skills and the Capgo MCP servers, an agent such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor can add plugins with the right native config, debug iOS and Android builds, request cloud builds, and upload live updates.
This guide explains why general agents get Capacitor wrong, how to set up skills and MCP in a few commands, prompts for each stage of the app lifecycle, and the guardrails that keep it safe.
Why general-purpose agents struggle with Capacitor
Agents are strong on web code. A Capacitor project adds a second half that changes every year:
Capacitor 8 changed Android SDK levels, defaults to Swift Package Manager for new iOS projects, and requires Xcode 26 for App Store uploads. Training data mixes Capacitor 3 to 8 advice.
. Agents often do only the JavaScript part.
Many community plugins are unmaintained. An agent picks whatever it saw most often, not what works on Capacitor 8.
Errors live in Xcode, Logcat, or a CI log, not in the editor.
You fix this with context the agent can load on demand, and tools it can call instead of guessing.
The toolkit: skills, MCP, and the CLI
Docs search, when-to-use guidance, OpenAPI location
Authenticated account actions: bundles, channels, builds
Same actions as shell commands, easy to review

The installer detects supported agents and places the skills where each one looks for them. The set covers plugin selection, best practices, Capacitor app and plugin major upgrades (including v7 to v8), CocoaPods to SPM migration, debugging, iOS and Android logs, push notifications, deep links, safe areas, security scanning, testing, CI/CD, App Store preflight, Cordova and web app migrations, Capgo live updates, and Capgo native builds. The
In Claude Code you can also use the plugin marketplace:

claude plugin marketplace add Cap-go/capgo-skills
claude plugin install capgo-cloud@capgo-skills
The public server needs no account. Add it to Claude Code:
claude mcp add --transport http capgo-docs https://capgo.app/mcp
The CLI server runs locally over stdio and uses your Capgo login, so log in first:

bunx @capgo/cli@latest login
claude mcp add capgo -- bunx @capgo/cli@latest mcp

Guardrails that keep agent work safe
Ask for a plan and a diff for anything under
Keep secrets out of the conversation.
Save build credentials and API keys yourself, git-ignore credential files, and never paste keys into prompts.
Use channels as a safety net.
Let the agent upload to a beta or internal channel. Promote to production yourself.
Capgo rolls a device back to the last working bundle if a new one fails to start, which limits the damage of a bad upload.
The CLI commands above are easy to read in the agent's log. If you are unsure what an MCP tool did, ask the agent to show the equivalent CLI command.
Agents can prepare builds and metadata. Submitting for review and answering reviewers should stay with a person.
Name it explicitly in the prompt, and check it was installed for that agent (rerun
succeeded in the same environment the agent runs in. Restart the agent after adding a server.
The agent suggests outdated Capacitor APIs.
Tell it your Capacitor version, and point it at the public MCP so it checks current docs.
Credentials are missing or the provisioning profile does not match the bundle ID. Re-save credentials and rerun the build request.
The bundle needs native changes. Ship a store build first, then the live update.

AI agents become useful for Capacitor once they stop guessing. Install the Capacitor skills so they follow correct procedures, connect the public Capgo MCP for docs and the CLI MCP for account actions, and keep a few guardrails around native changes, secrets, and production channels.
